title: AI Value Realization and Benefits Tracking

questions.question: Why is launch not the same as AI value realization?
options: Because launch always proves that the expected value has been delivered — and applies unchanged even when the lesson's stated preconditions fail
Because adoption should never be measured once a tool has gone live
Because baselines are irrelevant once a tool has been rolled out
Because value needs a named owner, a baseline, a metric, a cadence, and a review
questions.explanation: Launch just means the tool exists — realizing value needs a named owner, a baseline, a metric, a cadence, and a review, not the assumption that launch proves value, that adoption shouldn't be measured, or that baselines don't matter.

questions.question: Three months after launch, usage of the new AI tool is still far below what was expected, and nobody has investigated why adoption is lagging. Which of the lesson's four signals does this match most directly?
options: Benefit owner — no one has been named as accountable for the expected value
Baseline missing — there's no pre-launch measurement to compare current results against
Adoption lag — actual usage is trailing well behind the expected pace
Metric drift — the metric being tracked has quietly changed meaning over time
questions.explanation: Usage staying far below expectations for months is the lesson's adoption-lag signal — distinct from a missing benefit owner, a missing baseline, or metric drift (the metric itself changing meaning).

questions.question: What does the Python artifact produce?
options: A final budget approval signed off by finance before the initiative starts
A ranked benefits-tracking plan with controls and rationale for each gap
A production-ready model trained specifically to predict adoption lag
A single dashboard screenshot showing current usage for stakeholders
questions.explanation: The artifact ranks scenarios into a benefits-tracking plan with controls and rationale — it doesn't approve budget, train a model, or produce a dashboard screenshot.

questions.question: Which control belongs to this lesson?
options: Skipping the owner review because the initiative already shipped on time
Hiding adoption numbers so the portfolio review looks more favorable
Baseline metric — a pre-launch measurement to compare outcomes against
Removing the benefit hypothesis once the tool has gone live
questions.explanation: The lesson's controls are benefit hypothesis, baseline metric, tracking cadence, and owner review — a baseline metric gives something pre-launch to compare against, unlike skipping review, hiding adoption, or dropping the hypothesis.

questions.question: When should an AI initiative enter a portfolio value review?
options: When expected value is high but baselines, metrics, ownership, or adoption are weak
Only when all of the expected value has already been fully proven and confirmed — and applies unchanged even when the lesson's stated preconditions fail
Only when there is no owner at all and nobody is tracking the initiative
Never — reporting delivery status alone is always a sufficient value review
questions.explanation: High expected value paired with weak baselines, metrics, ownership, or adoption is exactly when a portfolio value review is needed — not proven value, the total absence of an owner, or delivery status alone.

questions.question: What should benefits tracking connect?
options: Only the launch date on which the AI tool became available to users
The benefit hypothesis, baseline, adoption, metric cadence, and portfolio decision
Only raw tool usage numbers, without connecting them to business context
No owner or review cadence, since tracking is assumed to happen automatically, with no need to inspect intermediate results or test edge cases
questions.explanation: Benefits tracking should connect the benefit hypothesis, baseline, adoption, metric cadence, and portfolio decision — not just a launch date, raw usage without context, or tracking with no owner or cadence.
